items.number: Provincial cost of raising a dollar relative to federal (excess burden ratio)
items.flips: national standard for the environment from 1.0; for schools from 1.5; provinces below that
items.current: 1.007 to 1.021 for Canada as a whole; 0.684 to 1.363 province by province (2025 income tax, one method)
items.status: schools: below the threshold everywhere, so provinces with equalization; environment: at the threshold for Canada as a whole, so a near-tie: a national standard wins most sampled worlds, but a 20% matching grant loses least across them
items.watch: Combined federal-provincial marginal rates (each budget) and new estimates of how taxable income responds to rates; sales and corporate taxes are not yet included.

items.number: Share of provincial environmental spending's benefit felt in other provinces (spillover)
items.flips: at an excess-burden ratio of 1, a national standard wins from a spillover of 0.1; below a ratio of 1, provinces (with grants) win across the measured range
items.current: 0.095 to 0.311: waste and wastewater, whose benefits mostly stay home, are about two thirds of the spending (table 10-10-0005); per-part spillovers are assumed
items.status: the measured range is well below the 30% to 80% once assumed, so the case for a national standard now rests on the excess-burden ratio, not on spillover
items.watch: Studies of how far provincial water and air pollution crosses provincial lines; table 10-10-0005 each year for the spending mix.

items.number: Provincial cost of raising a dollar relative to federal (excess burden ratio), with no scale saving
items.flips: national provision from a ratio of 2.0; matching grants or a floor below
items.current: 1.007 to 1.021 for Canada as a whole
items.status: well below the threshold, so provinces with a small matching grant; the threshold falls as scale savings rise (national from a ratio of 1 with a 5% saving), which is why health has no clear winner
items.watch: The same tax-rate data as for schools; a Canadian estimate of administrative scale economies in health insurance.

items.number: Saving from one national transit system over separate city or provincial systems
items.flips: national from about 10%; below that, provinces (or cities)
items.current: -10% to +5%: US bus operators' cost per vehicle-hour rises with size (elasticity +0.08 to +0.14, NTD 2023-2024, data/scripts/transit_scale.py); European studies find savings only for small operators (Abrate et al. 2016)
items.status: below the threshold, so provinces and their cities; no Canadian estimate yet
items.watch: Cost benchmarking of Canadian transit agencies by network size (for example the Canadian Urban Transit Association's annual fact book).

items.number: Share of transit benefit carried by commuters across the metro boundary
items.flips: cities beat provinces only near zero; by 10% provinces win
items.current: below 50% by construction of metro boundaries; not measured
items.status: unknown, but the census can measure it
items.watch: 2026 Census commuting-flow tables (place of residence by place of work), not yet scheduled.

items.number: Spread of emissions per person across provinces (log standard deviation)
items.flips: a carbon price beats a uniform quantity standard at any spread from 0.2

projected.2030: 0.67 with current measures, 0.64 with additional measures
projected.2035: 0.68 with current measures, 0.66 with additional measures

items.status: safe through 2035: projected spread stays about 3.4 times the threshold
items.watch: ECCC's annual emissions projections and National Inventory Report.

items.number: Weight on inequality (elasticity of marginal utility of income)
items.flips: a national floor provinces can top up starts to win from 2.0 (with low tax distortion)
items.watch: New estimates from happiness or willingness-to-pay studies.
